content.text: {"primary_meaning":"“Works” most commonly means a person’s deeds or conduct as the outward expression and moral fruit of inward faith, character, and allegiance. Good works are acts of obedience, love, justice, and mercy; evil works are sinful acts that manifest unbelief or corrupt desire. They are frequently portrayed as evidence by which persons are known and judged, although Christian traditions differ over their precise relation to salvation.","primary_basis":["Matthew 5:16 — good works visibly glorify the Father.","Matthew 7:16–20 — deeds are the “fruit” by which a person is known.","John 3:19–21 — evil deeds belong to darkness, while deeds done in God come to the light.","Romans 2:6–10 — God judges each person according to works.","Ephesians 2:8–10 — salvation is by grace through faith, and believers are created for good works.","Titus 2:14; 3:8 — redeemed believers are to be zealous and devoted to good works.","James 2:14–26 — works complete and demonstrate living faith; faith without works is dead.","Galatians 5:19–23 — the works of the flesh contrast with the fruit of the Spirit.","Revelation 2–3 — Christ repeatedly evaluates the churches by their works.","Revelation 20:12–13 — the dead are judged according to their works."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"In Catholic, Orthodox, and some Protestant accounts, grace-enabled good works are not merely evidence but genuinely cooperate in sanctification and bear upon final judgment and reward, without being independent achievements apart from grace.","basis":["Matthew 25:31–46","Romans 2:6–10","Philippians 2:12–13","James 2:14–26"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"In much Protestant interpretation, good works function primarily as the necessary fruit and evidence of justifying faith, not as its meritorious cause; evil works similarly disclose an unregenerate or disobedient condition.","basis":["Ephesians 2:8–10","Galatians 5:6","James 2:18","Matthew 7:16–20"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Paul’s phrase “works of the law” can refer specifically to deeds required by the Mosaic Torah rather than to all moral action. Many interpreters emphasize circumcision, food laws, and other Jewish covenant markers, while others understand the phrase more broadly as law observance undertaken for justification.","basis":["Romans 3:20,28","Galatians 2:16","Galatians 3:2–10","Philippians 3:4–9"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"In Johannine passages, the “works” of Jesus can mean his miracles, signs, and mission-deeds that testify to his divine authorization and identity, rather than moral works in general.","basis":["John 5:36","John 10:25,32,37–38","John 14:10–11"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"In apocalyptic and judgment texts, works may be understood as entries in a heavenly judicial record that disclose allegiance and determine judgment or reward.","basis":["Daniel 7:10","Matthew 16:27","2 Corinthians 5:10","Revelation 20:12–13"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"“Works” is sometimes treated as a symbol of self-righteous human effort or attempted salvation by personal achievement. This is influential in some evangelical preaching but is too broad if applied to every biblical occurrence of the word.","basis":["Romans 4:2–5","Romans 9:30–32","Philippians 3:7–9"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A fixed allegorical or esoteric meaning in which all references to works encode one particular institution, historical power, or hidden spiritual category.","basis":[],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a broad consensus that “works” ordinarily denotes deeds or conduct and often serves figuratively as the visible fruit of faith and character. There is no single settled symbolic interpretation applicable to every occurrence. Meaning depends especially on whether the context concerns good or evil conduct, “works of the law,” Jesus’ signs, sanctification, or final judgment; the relation of works to justification and salvation remains a major confessional difference."}
